transcript:
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Lynda Kenyon.
President Trump used what is known as a "pocket rescission" to cancel nearly $1 billion in
congressionally approved funding.
And Pierre's Eva Pukach reports.
The timing of the move just days before the fiscal year ends means Congress won't likely
have time to address the cuts before they go into effect.
The White House says the cuts focus on "wasteful and harmful government spending."
A majority of the cuts are to programs at the Department of Health and Human Services.
Others target education programs for migrant students, and a Department of Justice agency
focused on reducing racial tensions.
The pocket rescission drew bipartisan congressional backlash, including from Republican Senator
Susan Collins of Maine, who chairs the Senate Appropriations Committee, who said she would
work with her colleagues to address "these illegal actions."
Eva Pukach, NPR News.
Hurricane NOLO continues to meander south of Hawaii.
Forecasters say it could bring more than two feet of snow, of rain, rather, to the Big
Island, along with the dangerous flooding and mudslides.
NOLO is the third hurricane to batter Hawaii this year.
NPR's Juliana Kim reports.
Big Island and Maui are expected to see heavy rain and strong winds this weekend.
While the other islands may be spared from NOLO's harshest impacts, the entire state
is reeling from months of natural disasters, that includes major storms and an earthquake.
The state's governor, Josh Green, says over 1,200 homes have been damaged or destroyed
as a result.
He adds that recovery efforts will cost upwards of a billion dollars prior to NOLO.
Hurricane season in Hawaii is expected to last through November 30.
Juliana Kim, NPR News, Honolulu.
A new analysis of census data finds that for the fifth year in a row, the poverty rate
for seniors has risen.
NPR's Jennifer Luden reports.
The AARP Foundation analysis found women are far more likely than men to age into poverty,
and its own survey found just under a third of those 50 to 64 reported a significant drop
in household income in the past three months.
Foundation president Claire Casey says even a small disruption, like a car breaking down,
can be devastating for low-income workers.
You're much more likely to end up in the long term unemployed, and you're much more likely
to end up in a job that makes less than the one you were in.
A third of older low-income adults also said they did not have enough savings to cover
an emergency expense of $100.
Jennifer Luden, NPR News, Washington.
President Trump has rejected Iran's proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz.
The president told reporters outside the White House that Iran wanted the U.S. to lift its
blockade of Iranian ports, waive sanctions on oil, and observe a ceasefire that would
include Lebanon.
In addition, Iran said it would agree to talks in seven days.
You're listening to NPR.
Facebook, Instagram, YouTube, and TikTok are refusing to run advertisements for an upcoming
documentary on billionaire Elon Musk.
As NPR's Bobby Allen reports, Musk has threatened to sue over the nearly four-hour film, calling
it a hit job.
The documentary is called Musk, it's by Oscar-winning director Alex Gibney, and it's set for release
next month.
The film is a scathing look at the tech mogul's life from his childhood in South Africa, his
rise in Silicon Valley, including his takeover of the site formerly known as Twitter, along
with his time in the White House.
Gibney asks, "How did one man become so powerful?"
It's a message deemed too political by meta, YouTube, and TikTok, all of which have refused
to carry ads about the film.
That's according to a person close to the production who wasn't authorized to speak
publicly.
Earlier this month, lawyers for Musk threatened to file a defamation lawsuit over the film.
Musk would not sit for an interview with Gibney.
Instead, he used an AI-generated avatar of Musk as a stand-in.
Bobby Allen, NPR News.
Starbucks is planning to close 250 stores in North America.
Starting next week, the company did not say which coffee houses will close or how many
of them are in the U.S., it also did not say how many of the stores are unionized.
More than 700 U.S. Starbucks stores have voted to unionize since late 2021.
Starbucks Chief Operating Officer Mike Grahams did say the locations either are not delivering
acceptable financial results or they are not providing the experience he says the company
wants for its customers and employees.
I'm Lyndi Kenyon, NPR News in Washington.

topics.text: Trump cancels nearly $1 billion in congressionally approved funding using pocket rescission
Hurricane NOLO threatens Hawaii's Big Island with heavy rain, flooding, and mudslides
Poverty rate for seniors rises for fifth consecutive year, women particularly affected
Trump rejects Iran's proposal to reopen Strait of Hormuz and lift sanctions
Major social media platforms refuse to run ads for documentary about Elon Musk
Starbucks plans to close 250 stores in North America starting next week
